VisualArtifactSpec 1.0:
Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications

Shuyi Ouyang  Xiaojun Tang  Zijian Zou  Xintong Zhang Affiliation: Zhejiang University Affiliation: Accio Team, Alibaba Group    Mingli Song  Guannan Zhang  Hongwei Xue Affiliation: Zhejiang University    *Equal contribution Corresponding author
Abstract

Visual artifact tasks test agents’ ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model–harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

  
Project Page: https://accio-lab.github.io/VisualArtifactSpec
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/Accio-Lab/VisualArtifactSpec
HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Accio-Lab/VisualArtifactSpec

1 Introduction

Visual artifacts make an agent’s interpretation of a task concrete and inspectable. Presentations must develop an account across slides, animations must convey changes over time, and web interfaces must support browsing and interaction. These tasks share demands for source integration, content organization, and visual communication, but place different constraints on their execution. Evaluating multiple artifact families therefore helps determine whether an agent’s strengths extend across deliverable forms or remain concentrated in a particular medium.

Table 1 compares the artifact coverage and evaluation criteria of existing benchmarks. PresentBench (Chen et al., 2026), Code2Video (Chen et al., 2025), and Vision2Web (He et al., 2026) establish detailed protocols for presentations, educational videos, and websites, respectively. ArtifactsBench extends evaluation to multiple executable artifact types, including checks of instruction compliance, functionality, visual presentation, and content accuracy (Zhang et al., 2026). These advances leave a further evaluation need: systematically assessing how authoring choices serve different audiences, purposes, and media under a common framework across artifact families. Broad coverage, requirement satisfaction, and content accuracy alone do not establish whether the selected content, structure, and presentation are appropriate for the intended context.

We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Figure 1 shows representative artifacts from these four families. Task construction pairs source materials with authoring objectives, constraints, and required deliverables, while specifying the audience, purpose, and medium that inform both authoring and evaluation.

VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Shared criteria are instantiated through task-specific rating anchors informed by the audience, purpose, and medium. Figure 2 illustrates why these anchors matter: with the required information retained, content emphasis can support technical analysis or product promotion (A), information organization can provide a compact service overview or stepwise web guidance (B), and visual presentation can support flavor comparison or lifestyle appeal (C). Judgments link the criteria to source materials and native, rendered, temporal, or interaction evidence, making unmet requirements distinguishable from weaknesses in authoring choices.

Experiments with nine model–harness configurations show that high Task Fulfillment scores can coexist with deficiencies in Artifact Performance. The cross-family comparisons in Section 4.3 reveal strengths and weaknesses obscured by overall scores. The case studies in Section 5 connect score differences to evidence organization, mobile readability, and temporal consistency in the actual artifacts.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We construct VAS, a benchmark of 211 source-grounded creation and modification tasks across four artifact families, with explicit specifications of objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables.

  • •

    We develop an evidence-based evaluation protocol that separates Task Fulfillment from Artifact Performance, with task-specific rating anchors that instantiate shared Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium.

  • •

    We compare nine model–harness configurations across artifact families and connect their fulfillment and performance differences to observable authoring choices through artifact-based case studies.

2 Related Work

2.1 Visual Artifact Authoring and Benchmarks

GDPval evaluates professional work products, while AnalystBench studies reports grounded in multimodal sources (Patwardhan et al., 2025; Pham et al., 2026).

For presentations, AutoPresent introduces SlidesBench; PPTAgent assesses content, design, and coherence; and DeepPresenter refines rendered outputs (Ge et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026). PresentBench provides material-grounded checklists, while SlidesGen-Bench evaluates content, aesthetics, and editability (Chen et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026).

For graphics, ChartMimic evaluates chart-to-code generation, and Paper2Poster probes information conveyed by scientific posters (Yang et al., 2025; Pang et al., 2025). IGenBench and StructBench assess factual reliability, while BizGenEval checks commercial-image constraints (Tang et al., 2026; Zhuo et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). Image-level checks do not establish native-file editability or executable behavior. DrawAI explicitly evaluates reconstruction fidelity and editability (Cao et al., 2026); VAO-Bench assesses edits, dependent updates, and preservation through an image-only protocol (Guo et al., 2026). Graphic-Design-Bench covers layout, typography, infographics, design semantics, and animation (Deganutti et al., 2026b).

For animations and videos, Code2Video evaluates educational videos, while EvoPresent studies academic decks and presentation videos (Chen et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). Animation2Code evaluates appearance and temporal similarity; design-video metrics cover layout, motion, temporal quality, and content fidelity (Ji et al., 2026; Deganutti et al., 2026a).

For websites, Design2Code evaluates screenshot reconstruction, and DesignBench covers generation, editing, and repair (Si et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2025). Vision2Web tests static, interactive, and full-stack development; LongWebBench evaluates long-page structure and interactions (He et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026).

Across families, ArtifactsBench evaluates executable visual code using source code, temporal screenshots, and task-specific checklists (Zhang et al., 2026). VAS covers source-grounded creation and modification of both native and executable deliverables across four artifact families.

2.2 Rubric-Based Evaluation

Criterion design ranges from instance-specific quality criteria in BiGGen Bench to hierarchical requirement decomposition in PaperBench (Kim et al., 2024; Starace et al., 2025). In visual authoring, PresentBench aggregates binary judgments on instance-specific checklists, while ArtifactsBench scores task-specific criteria covering functionality and visual quality (Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). VAS separates binary Task Fulfillment checks from graded Artifact Performance ratings. Across artifact families, task-specific rating anchors connect shared Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery criteria to the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in artifact evidence.

Judge validation addresses a different question. MLLM-as-a-Judge and Judge Anything compare multimodal judgments with human assessments; RubricEval examines criterion-level accuracy in instruction following (Chen et al., 2024; Pu et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2026).

3 VisualArtifactSpec 1.0

3.1 Task Definition and Coverage

Each VAS task specifies an authoring objective, its intended audience, purpose, and medium, source materials, constraints, execution conditions, and required deliverables. Agents receive the instructions and inputs; evaluator-only materials provide reference facts, expected states, requirement checks, and rating anchors. Tasks cover creation, adaptation, revision, repair, and conversion, leaving content organization and presentation open within the stated requirements and modification boundaries.

Artifact families.

Table 2 summarizes the 211 tasks, and Figure 3 shows their hierarchical distribution. Presentations develop an account across slides; static graphics organize information on a single page or across a series; animations and videos develop content over time; web interfaces support browsing, exploration, tools, and workflows. Classification follows the principal deliverable objective rather than the file extension: HTML can encode slides, an animation, or a website. Appendix A.1 gives classification rules, formats, and task identifiers.

Purposes and audiences.

Figure 4 groups the tasks into eight application purposes, each describing what the artifact should accomplish for its users. Every task receives one primary purpose and a more specific use; Appendix A provides the mapping scope. Audience knowledge and needs shape the expected explanations, while medium and purpose shape information density, pacing, and presentation. For example, research communication emphasizes evidence and its limits, whereas practical guidance emphasizes actions and consequences. These distinctions inform task-specific evaluation criteria.

3.2 Task Construction

Figure 5 summarizes three stages that produced 211 tasks from 322 candidates.

Stage 1: Sources and feasibility.

We assemble public papers, reports, datasets, manuals, and media around concrete application objectives, retaining original files and source versions. Feasibility checks use rendering, native-file inspection, reproducible calculations, and temporal or interaction checks to establish usable inputs and observable outcomes. Controlled inputs supplement public sources for revision and repair: P03 supplies an earlier report grounded in official disclosures, and P26 supplies an animation with deliberate defects.

Stage 2: Task and reference construction.

We translate source facts and application needs into instructions, input contracts, reference facts, and task-specific rubrics. Input contracts distinguish supplied files from writable outputs; references record factual checks, expected states, and acceptable modification boundaries. Package checks verify required files, manifests, paths, and rubric structure. Source checks resolve discrepancies against originals and independently recompute required quantities; for example, P03 checks cover financial values, native tables, and slides that must remain unchanged. Rubric revisions are versioned with their task packages.

Stage 3: Execution and selection.

Agent trials expose ambiguous instructions, missing resources, observation failures, and artifact defects. Their results inform task revisions and checks of difficulty and score variation. Selection balances artifact and application coverage, evaluability, and source diversity. Same-source candidates are compared by their required operations and deliverables: creation and revision from the same materials can test different capabilities, whereas superficial variants add little coverage. Subsequent additions address gaps in artifact forms, authoring operations, and language coverage.

3.3 Evaluation Framework

VAS separates Task Fulfillment—Compliance (CP) and applicable Functionality (FN)—from Artifact Performance—Content (C), Organization (O), Visuals (V), and Delivery (D). The former verifies specified obligations; the latter assesses authoring quality through task-specific criteria within shared dimensions. Figure 6 summarizes the framework.

Requirement checks.

CP verifies explicit requirements such as required facts, formats, modification boundaries, and native editability. FN verifies required operations and observable outcomes, including state transitions and consistency after interaction. In the current collection, FN applies to the 60 web-interface tasks; the other 151 tasks use CP for requirement checks. CP and FN items form acceptance groups, each assigned to one dimension and fixed before agent comparisons.

Performance criteria and contextual anchors.

The 18 shared criteria comprise Content (3), Organization (3), Visuals (9), and Delivery (3), covering conceptual expression and evidence, structure and continuity, visual presentation, and usability and handoff. Table 5 defines their scopes. Task-specific anchors translate each scope into observable qualities for the intended audience, purpose, and medium. Table 3 illustrates this for V8. The distinction from requirement checks is explicit: in P35, CP verifies required samples and calculations, while C1 assesses how clearly the graphic explains means, valid sample counts, and observational limits to first-year students.

Each criterion receives an integer rating from −3-3 to +3+3. Negative ratings distinguish severe failure (−3-3), sustained impairment of major content or processes (−2-2), and localized substantive defects (−1-1). Zero denotes complete basic satisfaction without substantive defects, but ordinary quality. A rating of +1+1 denotes excellent execution with observable room for improvement; +2+2 requires full refinement across the applicable scope, with no substantive weakness or feasible task-relevant improvement of material benefit. A rating of +3+3 additionally requires a non-obvious design that resolves a real task challenge and yields substantial evidenced benefits beyond an equally correct, complete, and polished conventional solution. Appendix B.3 details rating evidence and item boundaries.

Evidence and judgment.

Evaluation freezes the submitted artifact and its file manifest, then combines source materials with rendered views, native-file inspection, temporal samples, and interaction records as required. Websites are inspected at 1440×9001440\times 900 and 390×844390\times 844 viewports and through required actions. A multimodal judge records item-level judgments with supporting pages, regions, timestamps, or interaction states, together with artifact, rubric, and judge versions. Unresolved evaluation failures remain unscored; Appendix B.1 specifies missing-artifact and website-failure handling. Section 4.1 gives the judge configuration.

We report the base BB, CP and applicable FN passed-group rates, C/O/V/D point scores, adjustment Δ\Delta, and total SS separately. Summaries use equal-task means and include task counts by family and purpose, along with completed, failed, and missing evaluations. Comparisons use common valid tasks under matching rubrics and scoring protocols; item-level evidence supports diagnosis beyond aggregate scores.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks and agents.

We evaluate nine model–harness configurations on the 211 VAS tasks: 47 presentations, 72 static graphics, 32 animations and videos, and 60 web interfaces. Each configuration receives the same task specifications and source materials, with evaluation rubrics withheld during authoring. All authoring configurations use their highest available reasoning setting. GPT-6 Astra, in a separate session with medium reasoning, serves as the common Agent Judge. Model identifiers, harness versions, reasoning labels, and detailed execution protocols are provided in the released repository.

Environment and protocol.

Runs use isolated Accio Linux sandboxes with a 7,500-second task-stage limit. Submissions, rubrics, and judge instructions are pinned for each evaluation round. TF uses the CP/FN objective groups in revision cp-fn-objectives-v2-20261114, with all child checks required to pass and equal weights across groups. Website inspection covers both 1440×9001440\times 900 and 390×844390\times 844 viewports and the required interactions; other artifacts follow the corresponding native-file, rendered, and temporal inspection requirements. Retained outputs are evaluated after authoring timeouts, and infrastructure or judge faults are handled separately from artifact defects.

Metrics.

Following Section 3.3, we report fulfillment base BB, performance adjustment Δ\Delta, and total score S=B+ΔS=B+\Delta, together with Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery (C/O/V/D). Overall means weight tasks equally. Family profiles use the corresponding task subsets; purpose-level summaries cover the 151 non-web tasks with task-level purpose labels. Full-dataset analyses use all 1,899 configuration–task results; a fixed subset of 38 tasks illustrates task-level AP distributions for all nine configurations. Detailed numerical results are provided in Appendix D.

4.2 Overall Performance

Overall differences are concentrated in Artifact Performance.

Figure 7 separates total scores into their two components. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol score 70.52 and 69.37, respectively, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 at 65.03. Across configurations, mean BB ranges from 41.96 to 49.51, while mean Δ\Delta ranges from 0.16 to 21.01. Of the 28.40-point total gap between GPT-6 Astra and Claude Sonnet 5, 20.85 points (73.4%) come from AP. Reporting the components separately therefore identifies whether a score difference primarily reflects unmet requirements or the quality of authoring choices.

Task Fulfillment and Artifact Performance reveal different limitations.

Task-level results further show that similar TF scores can accompany different AP outcomes. Across the full dataset, outputs with B=50B=50 span AP adjustments from −5.55-5.55 to 25.0025.00, revealing differences in authoring quality beyond requirement checks. Figure 8 illustrates this distinction on a fixed display subset of 38 tasks. Section 5 connects such differences to the underlying artifacts and task-specific criteria.

4.3 Performance across Artifact Families and Contexts

Aggregate rankings conceal family-specific profiles.

Figure 9(a) shows distinct profiles across artifact families. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 69.53 on static graphics but 57.05 on web interfaces; DeepSeek varies less, from 58.32 to 61.68 across the four families. GPT-6 Astra scores above 71 on presentations, static graphics, and animations/videos, compared with 67.20 on web interfaces. Cross-family evaluation therefore reveals both broad performance and strengths associated with particular deliverable forms.

Dimension profiles localize performance differences.

Figure 9(b) shows that GPT-6 Astra exceeds 20 points in all four AP dimensions. Gemini 4 Argon scores 9.94 in Delivery but 0.33 in Content and 0.09 in Visuals; Claude Sonnet 5 has positive Organization and Delivery scores but negative Content and Visuals scores. An accessible deliverable and a followable structure can therefore coexist with weaknesses in content or visual execution.

Purpose-level results in Table 10 further distinguish application settings. For example, DeepSeek scores 64.19 on promotion and engagement and 57.72 on practical guidance. These descriptive profiles combine differences in purpose, artifact family, and task difficulty. The cases in Section 5 examine audience and medium adaptation through specific rubric judgments and visible evidence.

4.4 Evaluation Analysis

Sensitivity to score aggregation.

We vary three aggregation choices while holding artifacts and item judgments fixed: a linear AP map 50​r/350r/3, equal C/O/V/D weights, and itemwise TF credit in place of grouped acceptance. Table 11 reports the results. Across the eight configurations compared under all three alternatives, the configuration ordering is preserved while score magnitudes change. Linear AP raises GPT-6 Astra by 7.31 points because it awards more points to +1+1 and +2+2 ratings. Equal AP weights raise Gemini 4 Argon by 2.22 points, reflecting its stronger Delivery and Organization scores. Itemwise TF raises Claude Sonnet 5 by 3.14 points by crediting passed checks within failed acceptance groups. These changes show how the aggregation rules control the contribution of intermediate quality ratings and incomplete acceptance objectives.

From aggregate scores to actionable evidence.

Criterion-level statistics in Appendix D.5 identify typography and legibility (V3) as the most frequent source of negative ratings, followed by traceability and handoff (D3), graphical craftsmanship (V6), and support for claims (C2). Section 5 relates these differences to evidence grouping in a research presentation, mobile reading in educational cards, and marker–curve consistency in a teaching animation.

5 Case Studies

We compare English-language artifacts from three tasks to relate recorded scores to visible authoring choices. Each pair receives the same fulfillment base; the cited AP criteria explain specific differences rather than the entire aggregate score gap.

5.1 Keeping Evidence Conditions with Research Claims

P01 requests an eight-slide ResNet presentation for a research-group meeting. GPT-6.1 Sol and DeepSeek both receive B=50B=50, with AP adjustments of 23.2023.20 and 13.6513.65. Figure 10 shows how their slides organize experimental evidence. Sol separates single-model validation from ensemble test results and attaches the protocol and split to each number. DeepSeek groups results from different settings under “Evidence at equal budget” with a shared “same depth / same parameters / same FLOPs” qualifier. Recovering the qualifier’s intended scope requires returning to an earlier slide. The local organization criterion O2 therefore assigns +2+2 and −1-1. For a research audience, preserving comparison conditions locally matters even when the requested results are present.

5.2 Adapting Complete Information to Mobile Reading

P99 requests five educational cards about hurricane forecast cones for a general audience reading on a phone. GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5 both receive B=50B=50, but their AP adjustments are 21.6521.65 and −5.55-5.55. Figure 11 compares their fourth cards at equal width. Sol separates the symbol classes into distinct bands with prominent definitions, while Sonnet distributes smaller explanations across a denser set of panels. At the prescribed 390-pixel inspection width, Sol’s supporting labels remain small (V3: −1-1); Sonnet’s necessary body and legend text repeatedly falls to roughly 5–8 pixels across the carousel (V3: −2-2). The comparison illustrates a medium-specific reading burden that is not resolved by including all required information, and also identifies a remaining weakness in the higher-scoring output.

5.3 Maintaining Correspondence through Motion

P121 requests a teaching animation of the first three standing-wave modes. Both artifacts receive B=50B=50, with AP adjustments of 22.3022.30 for GPT-6 Astra and −5.15-5.15 for Kimi K3. In Figure 12, Astra’s tracked material point remains on the second-mode curve, whereas Kimi’s point lies below it at the same instant. The temporal inspection also finds that Kimi’s three markers complete four cycles each over 4–20 seconds, although the curves complete four, eight, and twelve. This persistent mismatch yields −2-2 for both visual encoding (V4) and temporal rhythm (V8); Astra receives +2+2 and +1+1. The AP judgments reveal a temporal inconsistency not captured by the current TF checks, highlighting the need to verify marker–curve correspondence throughout the animation.

6 Conclusion

We introduced VisualArtifactSpec 1.0, a benchmark of 211 source-grounded creation and modification tasks spanning four artifact families and eight application purposes. VAS separates Task Fulfillment from Artifact Performance, using shared Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery criteria with task-specific rating anchors to assess authoring choices in context.

The results reveal substantial differences in Artifact Performance that Task Fulfillment alone does not capture. Family and purpose profiles reveal differences hidden by overall means, while artifact-based cases connect these differences to evidence organization, mobile readability, and temporal consistency. VAS thus provides a common framework for comparing authoring capabilities across artifact families and tracing performance limitations to concrete evidence. Future work should validate judge reliability and contextual ratings through human assessment and independent judges.

Appendix A Task Classification and Deliverable Formats

A.1 Classification Rules and Examples

Artifact families follow the principal deliverable objective, with secondary types listed in Table 2. Animated Graphics are standalone animated SVGs or looping GIFs; Animated Videos use authored diagrams, data graphics, or animation projects to produce a linear video; Edited Videos assemble supplied screenshots or media with timed focus, annotations, and captions. P25 is an Animated Video because it revises a re-renderable animation project, whereas P28 and P46 are Edited Videos that assemble interface screenshots into tutorials. Supplementary GIF previews do not create additional tasks.

For static graphics, multi-page series and explicit banner briefs take precedence; other single-page tasks distinguish focal-message posters from infographics and visual summaries, including evidence-led research posters.

Inputs and deliverable formats.

Inputs include papers, reports, data, manuals, images, media, templates, and existing projects. Required deliverables include PPTX, Beamer source, HTML or Markdown presentation source, ODP, SVG and raster exports, animation files, and website projects. Each task specifies its required combination of native files and rendered outputs; input formats and supplementary previews do not determine the artifact family.

Task identifiers.

The paper retains the original P-number shorthand for non-web tasks. Public identifiers preserve that number with an artifact-family prefix: for example, P80 is presentations-080, P99 is static-graphics-099, and P26 is animations-videos-026. Website identifiers run from web-interfaces-001 to web-interfaces-060 in sorted legacy-ID order. The accompanying task-purpose-mapping.json records all 211 identifier mappings and purpose assignments.

Application-purpose scope.

Each task is assigned one primary purpose according to its principal application objective, with a specific use within that category. Table 4 gives the distribution by artifact family. The 151 non-web assignments retain the established mapping; website assignments were reconstructed from task instructions and reconcile with the existing 60-task aggregate counts in Figure 4. The purpose-level results in Table 10 retain the 151 non-web-task analysis subset.

Appendix B Rubric Details

B.1 Dimension Scores and Exception Handling

Acceptance groups follow objectives such as deliverable completeness, editability, source attribution, modification boundaries, accessibility, and required operations. Explicit page or card boundaries guide the refinement of coarse groups; otherwise, items are grouped by acceptance objective. Each group belongs to CP or FN, with membership frozen before agent comparisons. All child items must pass for a group to pass. Groups share the 50-point base equally, irrespective of their item counts; CP and FN have no separate fixed point budgets.

For dimension d∈{CP,FN}d\in\{\mathrm{CP},\mathrm{FN}\} with nonempty group-index set 𝒥d\mathcal{J}_{d}, the dimension score is its passed-group percentage:

Scored=100​∑j∈𝒥dgj|𝒥d|.\mathrm{Score}_{d}=100\,\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{d}}g_{j}}{|\mathcal{J}_{d}|}. (5)

FN is omitted when no functional groups apply. For example, with ten acceptance groups, each failed group deducts five points from the base regardless of the number of failed child items.

Aggregation requires valid memberships and complete, evidence-supported judgments. Missing required artifacts receive No on affected requirements when inspection establishes their absence; unresolved assessments remain unscored. A website-specific exception applies when evaluator faults have been excluded and no usable website exists because the submission is missing, contains only descriptions or screenshots, or cannot run due to its own defects: all CP/FN items receive No and all performance items receive −3-3. Local failures affect only dependent items. This exception does not apply to other artifact families or evaluator environment failures.

B.2 Shared Performance Criteria

Table 5 defines the scopes of the 18 shared performance criteria. Each task instantiates these scopes through criterion wording, observation boundaries, and rating anchors tailored to its audience, purpose, and medium.

B.3 Rating Evidence and Item Boundaries

Judgments identify the observed property and its location in rendered views, native-file extracts, temporal samples, or interaction records. Positive ratings explain the design choice and its benefit: +1+1 also identifies the remaining limitation; +2+2 requires inspection across the full applicable scope and active checks for weaknesses; +3+3 additionally demonstrates how a non-obvious choice resolves a task challenge beyond a conventional solution of comparable correctness and polish. Sampling coverage is retained with the evidence.

Each item is judged within its own scope. Shared evidence supports multiple ratings only when it establishes an impact within each item’s boundaries. For example, reading contrast concerns V3, color-to-meaning correspondence concerns V4, and color harmony concerns V9. In modification tasks, evaluation covers permitted edits, their integration with retained content, and newly introduced defects; unchanged source defects and harmless style differences do not incur penalties.

B.4 Criterion Weights

Table 6 gives the weights used in Equation 3. Each rating is mapped through ϕ\phi before weighted averaging within its dimension. Thus, equally weighted ratings of 0 and +2+2 yield 12.5 points, rather than the 10 points obtained by mapping their mean rating. The criterion weights sum to 100, with dimension totals matching the C/O/V/D aggregation weights. The versioned scoring implementation and score-reporting conventions are available in the released repository.

Appendix C Benchmark Comparison Definitions and Evidence

Table 1 compares authoring evaluation protocols, including generation, editing, and reconstruction. For evaluation criteria, a check denotes routine assessment through a shared rubric or recurring checks across relevant task categories; isolated examples are insufficient. A dash denotes that routine assessment is not established. The TF/AP grouping organizes this comparison and need not reproduce a benchmark’s original scoring structure.

C.1 Coverage and Evaluation Criteria

Coverage follows the evaluated deliverable: P denotes complete presentation decks, G static graphics, M animations/videos, and W interactive web interfaces. Slide images and single-slide reconstruction do not establish P; static webpage renderings do not establish W.

Task Fulfillment.

Instruction compliance checks explicit content, structure, modification, and deliverable obligations. Functional verification checks operations and their resulting outputs or state transitions; rendering success alone is insufficient.

Artifact Performance.

Visual presentation covers appearance, layout, and legibility. Content accuracy covers factual and quantitative correctness, consistency of semantic relationships, and fidelity to source or reference content; visual resemblance alone is insufficient. Audience alignment assesses fit to readers’ prior knowledge and needs. Medium adaptation assesses fit to a medium or platform’s usage preferences through choices about information density, organization, pacing, and visual presentation. Prompt-level audience descriptions, responsive resizing, or general legibility alone do not establish these last two criteria.

These AP columns support cross-benchmark comparison. Content accuracy is assessed within VAS’s Content dimension; audience alignment and medium adaptation are expressed through task-specific C/O/V criteria. Organization and Delivery remain distinct VAS dimensions but are not independent columns in Table 1.

C.2 Evidence for Table Entries

Table 7 records the principal evaluation evidence and relevant scope boundaries. Paper section and table numbers refer to the cited benchmark reports. Released checklists provide additional evidence for PresentBench and ArtifactsBench.

VAS task-specific anchors.

P80’s research-group slides are assessed for a focal claim on each projected page and pauses between pages (V1, V8). P99’s social-media carousel is assessed for card-level entry points, information density, scanning sequence, and pacing across five cards (V8). These instantiate shared criteria for different readers and presentation practices.

Appendix D Supplementary Experimental Results

D.1 Overall and Family Scores

Tables 8 and 9 give the exact values underlying Figures 7 and 9. Task-level scores and scripts for reproducing the statistical figures and aggregate tables accompany the source release.

D.2 Application-Purpose Scores

Table 10 reports the 151 individually mapped non-web tasks across six purposes (Appendix A). Each column describes its task subset; artifact-family composition and difficulty also vary across columns.

D.3 Scoring Sensitivity

Table 11 isolates three aggregation choices while holding artifacts, item judgments, and all remaining scoring components fixed.

D.4 Matched Task Set

Figure 8 displays a fixed subset of 38 tasks shared by all nine configurations; the main findings use all 211 tasks. Table 12 lists their IDs. The panel contains 342 configuration–task results. Jitter separates points, and horizontal lines show observed ranges.

D.5 Criterion-Level Error Patterns

Criterion-level diagnostics use 1,688 assessments from eight configurations: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi K3, Gemini, and Claude Sonnet. Negative-rating rates are averaged over tasks within each configuration and then equally across configurations. The most frequent negative ratings occur for typography and legibility (V3, 52.31%), traceability and handoff (D3, 26.72%), graphical craftsmanship (V6, 25.06%), and support for claims (C2, 24.88%). Direct usability (D1) receives negative ratings in 2.43% of assessments. These rates distinguish the ability to deliver an accessible artifact from the readability, interpretability, and evidential support of its details.
